content:
As Israel continued its journey through the wilderness, another serious rebellion arose. This time the trouble did not begin with an enemy outside the camp. It came from within Israel itself, and even from among men who had already been given important responsibilities in Yahweh's service. Numbers 16 records the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, the involvement of two hundred and fifty respected leaders, Yahweh's judgment upon the rebels,
yet another rebellion by the congregation the very next day, and finally Aaron standing between the living and the dead as a plague spread through the camp. It is one of the most solemn chapters in the whole wilderness journey. Today let us look at the whole picture, before we begin studying it carefully, part by part, in the days to come.

Korah was not an ordinary Israelite. He was a Levite from the family of Kohath, and the Kohathites had already been given a very sacred responsibility.
They were appointed to carry the holy furnishings of the Tabernacle, after Aaron and his sons had covered them. This was an extraordinary calling,for the Kohathites carried the holy things through the wilderness, and therefore carried what represented the very presence of Yahweh among His people.Yet Korah was no longer satisfied with the position Yahweh had given him.He joined himself with Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, from the tribe of Reuben. And they were joined by two hundred and fifty leaders of the congregation, men of reputation and influence.Together they confronted Moses and Aaron, saying, "You take too much upon yourselves, for all the congregation is holy, every one of them, and Yahweh is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of God?" (Numbers 16:3). Their words sounded as though they were defending the congregation, but underneath them was a challenge against the very order that God Himself had established.

When Moses heard their accusation, he fell on his face. He did not immediately fight for his position or defend his reputation. Instead, he placed the whole matter before God. He told Korah and his company that Yahweh Himself would show who belonged to Him and whom He had chosen to come near. Korah and the two hundred and fifty were to take censers, place fire and incense in them, and stand before God. The question would not be settled by argument or by popularity. Yahweh would reveal whom He had chosen.
Then Moses spoke directly to Korah, reminding him of the privilege God had already given the Levites, for Yahweh had separated them from Israel and brought them near to serve the Tabernacle and minister before the congregation. And Moses asked a piercing question, "Is it a small thing to you?" (Numbers 16:9). Korah had received a holy calling, but he had begun to treat it as though it were too small. Then Moses exposed what Korah truly wanted, asking, "Are you seeking the priesthood also?" (Numbers 16:10). So, Korah's dissatisfaction with Aaron was, in the end, rebellion against Yahweh, because God was the One who had appointed Aaron.

Dathan and Abiram had a different complaint. When Moses called for them, they refused to come. They accused Moses of bringing them out of "a land flowing with milk and honey" only to kill them in the wilderness (Numbers 16:12-14). Shockingly, they were describing Egypt, the land of their slavery, with the very language Yahweh had used about the Promised Land. They also blamed Moses because they had not entered Canaan. But Moses was not the reason they had failed to enter the land. In Numbers 14, the people themselves had refused to believe Yahweh and go up when He commanded them.
Now they were blaming Yahweh's appointed servant for the consequences of their own rebellion. Moses became deeply grieved and brought the matter before God. The next day Korah and his company assembled at the entrance of the Tabernacle. The two hundred and fifty men stood with their censers, offering incense, while Korah gathered the congregation against Moses and Aaron. And then the glory of Yahweh appeared to all the congregation (Numbers 16:19).

Yahweh told Moses and Aaron to separate themselves, because judgment was coming. Yet once again the two men fell on their faces and interceded, pleading that the whole congregation should not perish because of the sin of those leading the rebellion. Yahweh then commanded the people to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, and Moses warned them not even to touch what belonged to these men. Dathan and Abiram came out and stood defiantly at the entrances of their tents with their households. Then Moses declared that Yahweh would give an extraordinary sign to prove that Moses had not acted out of his own ambition. If these men died an ordinary death, then Yahweh had not sent him. But if Yahweh did something entirely new, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, then Israel would know that these men had rejected Yahweh. And as soon as Moses finished speaking, the ground beneath them split apart. The earth opened and swallowed those connected with the rebellion, together with their possessions, and the surrounding Israelites fled in terror. At the same time, fire came out from Yahweh and consumed the two hundred and fifty men who had offered incense.

The judgment was directly connected to their sin. They had desired priestly privileges that Yahweh had not given them, and they had approached Him with censers of incense. So, their censers were not simply thrown away. God instructed Eleazar, Aaron's son, to gather the bronze censers from the fire, for they had become holy, having been presented before Yahweh. They were hammered into sheets and used as a covering for the altar, becoming a permanent memorial. Every Israelite who saw that altar was to remember that no unauthorized person should presume to offer incense before Yahweh and become like Korah and his company (Numbers 16:36-40). The very instruments through which they had challenged Yahweh's order became a lasting warning against repeating their rebellion. We might expect the chapter to end there. Surely, after seeing the earth open and fire come from Yahweh, Israel would never dare to rebel again. But astonishingly, the very next day, the congregation complained against Moses and Aaron, saying, "You have killed the people of Yahweh" (Numbers 16:41). They had seen God’s judgment with their own eyes, yet they blamed Moses and Aaron for it, and once more they gathered against them.

Then the cloud covered the Tabernacle, and the glory of God appeared again. Judgment began to fall, and a plague spread through the camp.
Moses immediately understood the seriousness of what was happening.He told Aaron to take his censer, put fire from the altar into it, add incense, and hurry into the congregation to make atonement for them. Aaron obeyed.The plague had already begun, but Aaron ran into the very midst of the people, offered the incense, and made atonement for them. And here Numbers 16 gives us one of its most powerful pictures, for "he stood between the dead and the living; so, the plague was stopped" (Numbers 16:48). The same priesthood that Korah had despised was now serving to preserve the lives of the congregation. The people had complained against Aaron. They had questioned his appointment. They had supported those who challenged his priesthood.Yet when judgment came, Aaron did not stand safely at a distance and watch them die. He ran into their midst and interceded for them. By the time the plague stopped, fourteen thousand seven hundred people had died, besides those who died in the rebellion of Korah. So the chapter that begins with men asking, "Why should Aaron have this position?" ends with Aaron standing between death and life for those very people. This chapter also shows us how rebellion grows, from Korah's dissatisfaction with his own calling, into jealousy and ambition, gathering others around a complaint, until an organized rebellion stood against Yahweh's servants. Beginning tomorrow, Yahweh willing, we will study Korah himself, the holy responsibility he had already been given, what he desired instead, and how dissatisfaction with a God-given calling grew into one of the greatest rebellions of the wilderness journey.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God, who appoints each of Your servants to their place,
Guard our hearts from the dissatisfaction that despises the calling You have given us.

Keep us from jealousy, ambition, and the gathering of complaints against Your order.

Teach us, like Moses, to fall on our faces before You rather than fight for our own place.

And we thank You for the priest who runs into the midst of the dying to intercede.

Let us never despise the very mercy that stands between us and the judgment we deserve.

"Let all that I am wait quietly before God, for my hope is in him." - Psalm 62:5

In Christ’s name, who stands between the dead and the living, we pray. Amen.
